extra_misconceptions.fact: Ultraviolet rays penetrate clouds and reflect off the water surface, while wind masks sweat loss and accelerates dehydration.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Cloudy skies and cool spray on a sailboat prevent severe sunburn and dehydration during a long day on the water.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Staying with the floating hull conserves body heat and gives rescue boats a much larger visual target to locate on open water.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Swimming toward a distant shore after a capsize is safer than staying with the overturned sailboat hull.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Vigorous rubbing drives cold blood from the extremities straight to the heart, which can trigger fatal cardiac arrest.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Rubbing the arms and legs of a hypothermia victim vigorously restores circulation and warms their core faster.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Outboard exhaust can pool around the transom and cockpit of an open boat when motoring slowly or idling with a tailwind.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Carbon monoxide poisoning only occurs inside enclosed cabin cruisers and never near open auxiliary sailboats.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to a sailor's core body temperature and motor control during the first fifteen minutes of cold-water immersion?
Which physical indicator distinguishes life-threatening heatstroke from heat exhaustion during an afternoon calm on open water?
Why is it dangerous to cleat the mainsheet tightly while sailing a light centerboard dinghy in gusty, shifty winds?
Where should a Scout position their head and torso during an unexpected jibe to prevent a severe boom strike injury?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Small-boat sailing requires completing the full 100-yard swimmer test before participating in the afloat merit badge requirements.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Passing the Scouting beginner swim test qualifies a Scout to crew a small sailboat without a swimmer on board.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Every participant must both pass the swimmer test and wear a Coast Guard-approved life jacket at all times while afloat.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Wearing a properly fitted life jacket replaces the requirement to pass the Scouting swimmer classification test.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The final 25 yards must be swum using an easy, resting elementary backstroke to demonstrate survival stamina in deep water.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The final 25 yards of the swimmer test can be completed using a fast breaststroke or freestyle sprint.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The swimmer must float on their back with minimal motion to prove they can rest and conserve energy while awaiting rescue.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Treading water vigorously for one minute satisfies the floating portion at the end of the Scouting swimmer test.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to a swimmer's energy reserves if they use an aggressive crawl stroke instead of the elementary backstroke?
Which physical indicator shows that a Scout's feet-first entry into deep water meets the Scouting swimmer test standard?
Why is it dangerous to board a tippy centerboard sailboat before verifying every crew member's current swimmer classification?
What measurement confirms that a candidate has completed both the strong forward stroke and resting backstroke segments?

extra_misconceptions.fact: A centerboard provides lateral underwater resistance to stop sideways drift while the crew's body weight balances the boat.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The centerboard on an unballasted dinghy acts primarily as a heavy counterweight that prevents the hull from capsizing.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Halyards hoist and lower the sails vertically on the mast, whereas sheets control the horizontal trim angle of the sails.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Halyards and sheets are interchangeable terms for any line used to trim the angle of the sails to the wind.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Pushing the tiller to starboard angles the rudder blade to port, which pivots the stern right and turns the bow to port.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Pushing a sailboat's tiller to the right turns the bow of the boat to the right just like a bicycle handlebar.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Sailboards are explicitly excluded by the merit badge standards because they lack a cockpit, rudder, and standard rigging.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A windsurfer or sailboard satisfies the craft requirements for demonstrating Small-Boat Sailing merit badge skills.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to a sailboat's sideways leeway when you raise the centerboard completely while sailing close-hauled?
Which structural difference separates the role of standing rigging from running rigging on a Marconi-rigged sloop?
Under what condition does pushing the tiller toward the port gunwale cause the bow of the boat to turn to starboard?
Why is it dangerous to rig a sailboat with worn clevis pins or missing cotter rings on the shrouds and forestay?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Small sailboats must give way to large vessels restricted to narrow channels and commercial craft unable to maneuver easily.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A sailboat under sail always has the right-of-way over every power-driven vessel in a narrow shipping channel.

extra_misconceptions.fact: On the same tack, the windward boat is the give-way vessel and must keep clear of the leeward stand-on sailboat.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: When two sailboats on the same tack converge, the windward boat has the right-of-way and holds its course.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Safety Afloat mandates that every participant wear a properly fitted Coast Guard-approved life jacket at all times afloat.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Stowing life jackets unlocked beneath the cockpit seats satisfies Safety Afloat rules during calm summer weather.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Reefing reduces the exposed sail area and lowers the center of effort so the boat stays controllable in heavy gusts.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Reefing the mainsail increases the sail area so a boat can outrun an approaching thunderstorm back to the dock.

extra_socratic_questions: Under what condition does a sailboat on port tack become the give-way vessel when converging with another sailboat?
Which physical indicator in the western sky warns a crew to reef sails or head for shore before a squall line hits?
What measurement confirms that your supervisory ratio complies with Scouting America Safety Afloat rules for ten boats?
Why is it dangerous to launch a sailing excursion without filing a detailed float plan with a responsible person ashore?

extra_misconceptions.fact: A masthead fly on a moving boat indicates apparent wind, which blends true wind with the headwind created by boat speed.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A masthead wind indicator on a moving sailboat points directly toward the true geographic wind direction.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Hoisting downwind fills the sail immediately with pressure; sails must be hoisted with the bow pointed straight into the wind.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Hoisting the mainsail while the boat is pointed dead downwind keeps the sail quiet and easy to control.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Dark, rippled patches called catspaws mark where gusts strike the water, while glassy areas indicate calm wind lulls.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Smooth, glassy patches on a lake surface show where the strongest wind gusts are touching down on the water.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Luffing windward telltales show you are pinching too close to the wind or need to trim the sheet in slightly.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Fluttering windward telltales on a close-hauled jib mean the sail is sheeted in too tightly and stalling.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to the apparent wind direction relative to the bow when your sailboat accelerates onto a fast beam reach?
Which physical indicator on the water surface reveals an approaching gust and its wind direction before it hits your sails?
Where should a Scout position the bow while hoisting the mainsail at a mooring to prevent the boat from surging forward?
Under what condition does the leeward telltale on a jib stall and flutter while the windward telltale streams smoothly aft?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Running downwind requires easing the sails out nearly perpendicular to the hull to catch the full push of the wind.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Pulling the sails in tight against the centerline produces maximum boat speed when sailing dead downwind on a run.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Approaching a dock on a downwind run prevents luffing the sails to stop; always approach on the leeward side into the wind.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Approaching a dock under sail with the wind directly at your stern makes stopping at the pier much easier.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Righting a capsized dinghy requires standing on the centerboard to lever the hull upright while uncleating the sheets.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Righting a capsized dinghy requires climbing onto the high gunwale and pulling upward on the mast.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Pointing into the no-go zone stalls the sails in irons; a boat must tack at forty-five-degree angles to work upwind.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Sailing straight into the no-go zone allows a sailboat to make the fastest progress toward an upwind mark.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to a sailboat's forward momentum if the helmsman pushes the tiller over too hard and stalls the rudder?
Where should a Scout position the centerboard and sheets when transitioning from a close-hauled beat to a broad reach?
Why is it dangerous to let the boom swing uncontrolled across the cockpit when jibing on a downwind run?
Which sequence of maneuvers brings a sailboat alongside a floating victim in the water with minimal forward speed?

extra_misconceptions.fact: A square knot capsizes and slips easily under heavy or uneven tension and should only bind light reef points or sail covers.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A square knot is the safest knot for tying a mooring line around a piling or joining two heavy towlines.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A bowline forms a secure fixed loop that never slips under load yet breaks open easily by pushing the back of its collar.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A bowline tightens down permanently under a heavy sailing load and must be cut free with a rigging knife.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Securing the bitter end under your foot or in your non-throwing hand prevents a heavy pull from dragging you overboard.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Wrapping a heaving line around your wrist ensures you do not drop the bitter end while throwing it to a dock.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Twisted nylon stretches significantly to absorb anchor shock, whereas low-stretch braided polyester keeps sails properly tensioned.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Three-strand twisted nylon line and braided polyester line have identical stretch characteristics for sailboat halyards.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to a square knot when you use it to join two lines of unequal diameter under a heavy sailing load?
Why is it dangerous to finish a cleat hitch on a halyard with multiple locking half hitches stacked on top?
Which physical indicator shows that a faked-down mooring line on the foredeck will run out free without tangling?
Under what condition does a figure-eight stopper knot prevent a jib sheet from pulling back through its fairlead block?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Repeatedly creasing a sail in the same spots breaks down the resin coating; rolling sails or varying fold lines prevents wear.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Folding a Dacron sail along the exact same crease lines every trip keeps the cloth stiff and extends its service life.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Chlorine bleach and stiff bristles degrade synthetic sail fibers and UV stitching; clean sails only with mild soap and water.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Washing Dacron sails with household bleach and a stiff deck brush removes mildew without harming the sailcloth.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Direct sunlight rapidly degrades Dacron fibers and thread through UV exposure unless protected by a sail cover or storage bag.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Leaving sails furled uncovered on the boom all summer protects them from moisture better than storing them in a bag.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Removing the drain plug and elevating the bow allows trapped moisture to drain out so freezing water cannot crack the hull.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Sealing the hull drain plug tightly during outdoor winter storage prevents rainwater and snowmelt from entering the boat.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to Dacron sailcloth fibers and stitching when sails are stuffed wet into a bag after sailing in saltwater?
Which physical indicator on a stainless steel shroud swage fitting reveals hidden crevice corrosion before a mast failure?
Where should a Scout position padded supports under a fiberglass hull when storing a small sailboat for the winter?
Why is it dangerous to tow a boat trailer in the spring without inspecting and repacking the wheel bearings after launch use?

extra_misconceptions.fact: No sailboat can sail directly into the no-go zone; close-hauled boats must sail roughly 45 degrees off the true wind.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A close-hauled sailboat can point directly into the eye of the wind if the mainsheet is trimmed completely tight.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Halyards hoist and lower the sails vertically, whereas sheets trim the horizontal angle of the boom or clew to the wind.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Halyards and sheets are interchangeable lines used both to hoist sails up the mast and to trim their angle to the wind.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A catboat is a single-hulled vessel with one mast stepped far forward and a single sail, while a catamaran has two hulls.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The term catboat refers to a twin-hulled catamaran rather than a single-masted monohull rigged with only one sail.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A centerboard resists leeway sideways drift only; crew weight on the windward rail provides the righting moment in a dinghy.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: An unballasted centerboard provides the same heavy counterweight against capsizing as a lead-ballasted fixed keel.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to the boom and centerboard positions as a skipper bears away from close-hauled to a broad reach?
Which structural feature distinguishes a fixed-keel monohull from a centerboard dinghy or a multihull catamaran?
What wind-angle measurement relative to the bow confirms a sailboat has entered the no-go zone instead of a close reach?
Why is it dangerous to sail on a dead run without watching the leech and telltales for signs of an accidental jibe?
